items.name: palamim/starboard
items.description: A macOS terminal that sits permanently beside the Dock instead of appearing on a hotkey. It stays on screen across every Space, including over full screen apps, and never takes focus from whatever you are working in. Inside it is a real login shell, so directory, history and state carry between commands rather than each one starting fresh. The bet is that a terminal you glance at gets used differently from one you summon.

items.name: Parchment: Agenda & Daily Note
items.description: A private daily journal for iPhone that keeps writing, plans, calendar entries and reminders in one place rather than splitting them across four apps. The category is crowded, so what matters for an app like this is whether the calendar integration is good enough to replace the separate planner people already use.

items.name: DramaWave - Dramas & Reels
items.description: A streaming app for vertical short dramas, the soap opera episodes shot in portrait and cut into two minute instalments, in the same category as ReelShort and DramaBox. The format is bought heavily through social advertising, so the numbers on apps like this move with marketing spend more than with word of mouth.

items.name: Claude by Anthropic
items.description: Anthropic's Claude application for iPhone and iPad. As an entity here it is useful mainly as a control: a major model provider's consumer app is not an unknown rising, so movement on it measures how the App Store charts respond to a release rather than anything about early adoption.

reflex-dev/xy
items.brief: 13,544 weekly downloads, up 11.5% in a day and 200% since 4 August, while stars moved 0.5%. Seventh straight appearance, and the gap between installing it and bookmarking it has never once closed.
items.description: A charting library for Python, from the team behind the Reflex web framework. It renders interactive charts directly from Python objects, so the analysis and the chart live in the same place instead of the data being handed to a JavaScript layer to draw. It ships on PyPI, and that is what makes the adoption measurable: a download is someone installing it into a project, a star is someone bookmarking it, and those two numbers have been moving in opposite directions here for two weeks.

items.name: TheRealYT/git-knife
items.brief: 291 stars, up 12.3%, with 165 HackerNews points and 101 comments. Open issues up 33.3% on the same day: the people who found it are using it hard enough to file bugs.
items.description: A desktop GUI for editing git commit metadata: the message, the author, and both the author and the committer dates. Existing git interfaces reword and reorder commits well but treat dates as fixed, and the tools that can rewrite them, git-filter-repo and commit-tree, have no interface at all. git-knife covers that gap by shelling out to the system git and rebuilding each commit from its original tree, so file contents are provably never altered.

items.name: antigma.ai
items.brief: Forks up 30.8% against stars up 12.7% in a day, 50 forks on 1,652 stars. Pushed the same day, and HackerNews has gone quiet at 1.8%, so the growth is running without a thread behind it.
items.description: Antigma, a terminal harness for running AI coding agents, published as the repository AntigmaLabs/ante. The agent loop, the tool calls and the sandbox ship in a single binary rather than being assembled from separate services, so the whole run happens on one machine and can be inspected afterwards. For a tool of this kind the fork count is the number that carries information: forking means taking the code away to change it, which is a different act from starring it.

still_moving.name: antirez/h3.c
still_moving.brief: Stars up 117%, forks up 96%, open issues up 183% and HackerNews comments up 453% in a single day. 71 forks on 1,432 stars is a 5% ratio within hours, and 13 open issues means people are running it on their own machines rather than reading the README.
still_moving.description: An inference engine written in C that runs the MiniMax H3 language model on Apple hardware, from Salvatore Sanfilippo, who wrote Redis. Its claim is that a model this size can be served from one self contained C program with no Python runtime and no framework at all. That matters because the usual stack is several gigabytes of dependencies before the model itself is even loaded.

still_moving.name: palamim/starboard
still_moving.brief: Second appearance, and stars, forks and open issues all moved together again at 3.1%, 3.6% and 20%. Pushed today rather than abandoned after the thread. At this size that is a handful of people, and it is the same handful coming back.
still_moving.description: A macOS terminal that sits permanently beside the Dock instead of appearing on a hotkey. It stays on screen across every Space, including over full screen apps, and never takes focus from whatever you are working in. Inside it is a real login shell, so directory, history and state carry between commands rather than each one starting fresh. The bet is that a terminal you glance at gets used differently from one you summon.

still_moving.name: MakazhanAlpamys/Soup
still_moving.brief: 68 open issues against 430 stars is a 16% ratio, five times what a young repo usually carries, and forks are up 5.5% against 3% star growth. The people arriving are running it and hitting walls rather than bookmarking it. HackerNews has gone quiet at 0.7%.
still_moving.description: Fine tunes a large language model from a single YAML file, with no SSH into a training box and no framework configuration to assemble. It streams layers rather than loading the whole model, which is what lets an 8 billion parameter model train on a laptop GPU with 4 GB of memory. Distributed on PyPI as soup-cli, so installs are countable separately from stars.

still_moving.name: t8y2/dbx
still_moving.brief: Third appearance. 13,242 stars with 1,344 forks is one fork per ten stars, where most repos manage one in fifty, and the ratio has held for a week rather than spiking and fading. Homebrew installs are the number to watch, because a package manager install puts it on a machine.
still_moving.description: A desktop database client that speaks to more than 70 systems, MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite, Redis, MongoDB, DuckDB and SQL Server among them, in a 20 MB download. The same build ships as a desktop app, a Docker image and a command line tool, with an AI assistant and an MCP server included. Most clients of this scope are hundreds of megabytes, so the size is the claim being made.

still_moving.name: runtimewire.com
still_moving.brief: Pricing tiers up 33.3%, which means it added a plan, and a new plan is the monetisation trigger this system treats as a signal on its own. On the HackerNews front page the same day with 22 comments.
still_moving.description: A news site covering the AI industry as it happens: funding rounds, model launches, infrastructure changes and founder moves, filed as short scoops rather than weekly summaries. It competes on speed of publication against the general technology press, so the interesting measurement for a site like this is whether readers arrive directly or only through aggregators.

still_moving.name: xoreaxeaxeax/asm-hall-of-shame
still_moving.brief: Stars up 38.4% in a day, forks up 12%, open issues up 20%, with GitHub, HackerNews and Lobsters all seeing it at once. Lobsters points more than doubled at 108.8%. Five forks on 567 stars this early says people are submitting entries, not just reading them.
still_moving.description: A leaderboard for the slowest possible single machine instruction, from the reverse engineer behind the sandsifter processor fuzzer. Instruction analysis normally chases speed; this deliberately searches for the floor. The current x86 champion takes 198 billion cycles, about 62 seconds, by making one instruction load processor state across a deliberately saturated PCIe fabric. Setup can be anything, but only one instruction is scored.

still_moving.name: V4bel/Zapscape
still_moving.brief: Three independent collectors on day one, GitHub, HackerNews and Lobsters at once. Stars and forks both up 12.9% in exact lockstep, with Lobsters comments up 25%. Ten forks on 110 stars this early says people are running the exploit to see it work.
still_moving.description: A working exploit and write up for CVE-2026-64561, a guest to host escape in KVM on x86. The bug is a use after free in the shadow MMU, in the recursive path that runs when shadow pages are reclaimed, and a guest can trigger it alone to reach the host kernel with root privilege. It is the third in a series from the same researcher, published after the coordinated embargo ended.

still_moving.name: pg83/shitty
still_moving.brief: Fourth day and the shape has held. Open issues up 42.9% against 2% star growth, long after HackerNews stopped talking, where comments moved 1.2%. Most launch driven repos flatten within seventy two hours. This one kept the adoption after losing the audience.
still_moving.description: A terminal emulator built for low latency and fast startup, keeping terminal state on the CPU and rendering cells through Vulkan on Linux and Metal on macOS. The README publishes head to head throughput against ghostty, alacritty and kitty with every terminal equalised first, which is unusual enough to be worth noting. The same code ships under two names for people who would rather not type the first one.

still_moving.name: veedstudio/open-edit
still_moving.brief: Second day and the ratios held. Stars up 8.2%, forks up 12.1%, with forks again outpacing stars: 141 stars and 8 forks yesterday, 172 and 12 today. At that size a dozen people move it, so the direction carries the information rather than the magnitude.
still_moving.description: An open source video editing pipeline from VEED that has no timeline and no interface. Editing happens entirely through a coding agent: cut and reframe footage, layer motion graphics, turn slides or web pages into video. Source footage is optional, since stills and generated media are enough for some briefs. The renderer is free to use but closed, while everything driving it is open.
